slides.title: Understanding and Procuring Open Technologies and Products
slides.subtitle: Understand what is open, what it costs, and who will keep it working.
slides.transcript: Open technology gives you more ways to use, adapt, and improve a product. A good purchase turns those possibilities into something your team can run and support.

source_refs.basis: Single-module editorial revision; original teaching retained or consolidated.

slides.title: Open means permission
slides.transcript: Open technology gives you rights to use, study, change, and share work under its license. It does not mean everything is free. Making hardware, connecting systems, and keeping them running still take people and money.

figure.caption: Know what you can do with the technology, and what it will take to use it.

slides.title: Openness takes different forms

cards.title: Software
cards.body: Code you can study, use and change under its license.

cards.title: Hardware
cards.body: Design information for studying, changing and making hardware.

cards.title: Data
cards.body: Information available for reuse under stated terms.

cards.title: Standards
cards.body: Shared specifications for interfaces and formats.

slides.transcript: Open software shares code. Open hardware shares design information. Open data permits reuse, and open standards describe common interfaces or formats. Check what is actually available and what its terms allow. A product can follow an open standard without sharing its hardware design.

source_refs.basis: Single-module editorial revision; original teaching retained or consolidated.

slides.title: From shared programs to shared infrastructure
slides.transcript: Early computing communities shared programs and ideas. The free software movement made user freedoms explicit. Copyleft licenses helped keep those freedoms in shared changes. In nineteen ninety-eight, the Open Source Initiative helped bring this approach to business. Today it reaches hardware, data, AI models, and standards too.

figure.caption: Collaboration grew from software into many kinds of technology, including AI models.
figure.alt: From shared programs to shared infrastructure

slides.title: Read the license before you commit

cards.title: Strong copyleft
cards.body: GPL and AGPL: sharing duties depend on the license and use.

cards.title: Limited copyleft
cards.body: LGPL, MPL and EPL: duties apply within defined boundaries.

cards.title: Permissive
cards.body: MIT, BSD and Apache: broad reuse, with conditions such as notices.

slides.transcript: Strong copyleft can require sharing covered source when software is distributed. The Affero license also covers certain uses over a network. Limited copyleft applies within narrower boundaries. Permissive licenses usually allow proprietary versions, with conditions such as keeping notices. Record each license version and how you will modify, combine, host, or distribute the work. Have your legal team review those details before you commit.

slides.title: Count the cost of keeping it working
slides.transcript: A low purchase price is only the beginning. Count integration, testing, people, tools, manufacturing, shipping, spare parts, upgrades, and eventually moving to something else. Reuse and a choice of support providers may save money. Compare complete alternatives over the same period.

figure.caption: Compare purchase, operation, support and change over the same period.
figure.alt: Count the cost of keeping it working

slides.title: Make the benefits real

cards.title: Reuse
cards.body: Build on tested components and common interfaces.

cards.title: Adapt
cards.body: Change the technology to meet a real need.

cards.title: Inspect
cards.body: Review the code or design and test the result.

cards.title: Improve together
cards.body: Share fixes and explore better use of equipment and energy.

slides.transcript: Shared building blocks can simplify a system. Visible code and designs let people adapt, inspect, and improve it. Communities can solve problems together, including better cooling, power use, repair, and reuse. These benefits still need skilled people and testing. Measure results in your own setting; another deployment’s savings are not a promise.

slides.title: Keep your choices practical
slides.transcript: Permission to switch suppliers helps only if another supplier can deliver. Check compatible parts, support, stable interfaces, and the knowledge your team needs to make a change. Open standards can help systems work together, but you still need to test the exact combination.

figure.caption: Real alternatives need compatible technology, available suppliers and a workable change plan.

slides.title: Look at what supports the product
slides.transcript: Stable technology makes change easier. Clear licensing explains your rights and duties. An active community helps maintain and improve the work. Together, these foundations can support lower cost, adaptable designs, transparency, and more supplier choice. Check each foundation before relying on the promised benefits.

figure.alt: Look at what supports the product
figure.caption: Stable technology, clear rights and an active community support lasting value.

slides.title: Seven checks before buying

cards.title: Cost
cards.body: Include the full cost of use and eventual change.

cards.title: Design flexibility
cards.body: Check what you can change and how quickly.

cards.title: Stability
cards.body: Look for reliable interfaces, upgrades and tests.

cards.title: Transparency
cards.body: Confirm what you can inspect.

cards.title: Supplier choice
cards.body: Check availability and realistic alternatives.

cards.title: Rights and community
cards.body: Two checks: suitable license terms and active, well-run collaboration.

slides.transcript: Check total cost, design flexibility, stability, transparency, supplier choice, licensing, and community activity. Use the assessment checklist to record evidence and unresolved questions. Give the most weight to what your project needs. Name someone to follow up on gaps, and revisit the assessment when the technology or your plans change.

slides.title: Plan the whole life of the system
rows: Install, connect and check the system
slides.transcript: Agree the work before choosing who will do it. For a server, that means planning the rack, power, and cooling; testing firmware, drivers, and performance; installing and accepting the system; then maintaining it. At every stage, identify any customization and the skills needed. A missing task becomes someone’s problem later.

source_refs.original_title: Make an OCP server plan concrete
source_refs.basis: Single-module editorial revision; original teaching retained or consolidated.

source_refs.original_title: Define the work before choosing a supplier
source_refs.basis: Single-module editorial revision; original teaching retained or consolidated.

slides.title: Decide who does the work
slides.transcript: An in-house team keeps direct control but needs the skills and time. An external supplier adds expertise, with more dependence on that supplier. A hybrid approach shares the work. Agree who tests, accepts, supports, and documents each part. Make handoffs and knowledge transfer clear, so no responsibility falls between teams.

figure.caption: Keep the work in-house, use a supplier, or share it with clear responsibilities.

entries.text: Start with lifecycle requirements, then assign responsibilities.

slides.title: Know what you are paying for

cards.title: Open core
cards.body: An open foundation with paid features. Check which features you need.

cards.title: Managed hosting
cards.body: A supplier runs the service. Check data export and your ability to move.

cards.title: Professional support
cards.body: Pay for integration, training or support. Keep useful knowledge in your team.

slides.transcript: Open core adds paid features to an open foundation. Managed hosting pays a supplier to run a service. Professional support pays for expertise. Check essential paid features, data export and the cost of moving, and the knowledge your team will keep. For hardware, also identify the manufacturer, available product, design information, and support terms.

source_refs.original_title: Commercial models answer a different question
source_refs.basis: Single-module editorial revision; original teaching retained or consolidated.

slides.title: Choose how to take part
slides.transcript: The Open Technology Game describes five levels: adopting, contributing, steering, mobilizing, and projecting. They range from using open work to helping shape it across communities. Mobilizing and projecting are separate levels, even where shown together. This is a way to describe participation, not an OCP membership ladder. Higher is not always better.

figure.caption: Five levels describe ways to participate, not membership ranks.

slides.title: Use well, then give something back

cards.title: Adopting
cards.body: Understand the terms, connect the technology and support it.

cards.title: Contributing
cards.body: Share useful work with clear approval, ownership and community relationships.

slides.transcript: Adopting means using open work well, with the right permissions, skills, and support. Contributing means making something others can use. Give contributors clear approval, priorities, and time. An open source program office or another named owner can help. Small, useful contributions can improve the technology you depend on and build trust.

source_refs.basis: Single-module editorial revision; original teaching retained or consolidated.

slides.title: Grow your involvement with care

cards.title: Steering
cards.body: Help guide plans, governance and contributions.

cards.title: Mobilizing
cards.body: Bring people together around open alternatives.

cards.title: Projecting
cards.body: Connect openness across technologies and communities.

slides.transcript: Steering means helping guide a project’s plans and decisions. Mobilizing brings people together around open alternatives. Projecting connects that work across areas such as software, hardware, data, and standards. Each takes time and trust. Choose a role you can sustain, with named people and resources, while respecting the community’s shared purpose.

source_refs.basis: Single-module editorial revision; original teaching retained or consolidated.

slides.title: What matters most
items: Check rights, evidence and the full cost.
Plan who will build, run and support the result.
Keep real choices and take part at a level you can sustain.
slides.transcript: A sound open-technology purchase brings together rights, evidence, and a workable plan. Know who will keep it running, keep your options practical, and contribute where you can.

term_glossary.tooltip: License conditions that preserve specified sharing rights in covered derivatives. The obligations depend on the exact license, version and use.
A license that generally permits proprietary derivatives while retaining conditions such as notices or attribution. Review the exact terms.

lms_catalog.title: Understanding and Procuring Open Technologies and Products
lms_catalog.short_description: Understand open technology, compare the full cost, and choose how to buy, support and contribute.
lms_catalog.overview: A good purchase of open technology starts with what you can use and change, then follows through to the people and support that keep it working. Explore how to assess those choices and take part in the communities behind the technology.
lms_catalog.duration_note: Includes narration, teaching videos, reading and the final two-question check. Exploring linked resources or inspecting figures in detail may take longer.

modules.summary: Explore openness in software, hardware, data, AI models and standards. Learn how license terms, full costs, supplier choices and community activity shape a purchase. Use seven practical checks, plan the work across the life of a system, compare delivery and payment models, and consider five levels of community participation.
